newsitem.title: USA: S&P raises Clark Cty, Nev., highway revs to A-plus.
newsitem.headline: S&P raises Clark Cty, Nev., highway revs to A-plus.

text.p: Standard & Poor's today has assigned its single-A'-plus rating to Clark County, Nev.'s $70 million highway revenue (motor vehicle fuel tax) improvement bonds series 1997 dated April 15, 1997, which are scheduled to sell April 15, 1997.
At the same time, Standard & Poor's has raised its rating on the county's $7.87 million highway improvement motor vehicle fuel tax revenue bonds to single-A'-plus from single-A'.
The rating upgrade on Clark County's highway revenue bonds reflects the following credit strengths:
-- Good growth in the pledged revenue stream, as exemplified by steady increases in fuel sales over the last five years;
-- A rapidly growing economic base with a demonstrated ability to maintain and expand visitor market share despite increased gaming competition across the U.S.,
-- Continued healthy debt service coverage; and

Credit concerns include a local economic base that is heavily concentrated in gaming; and the potential for lower-than-expected fuel sales growth due to the inability to predict demand patterns. Proceeds of the 1997 bonds will be used to fund various street and highway projects within the county. Debt service is payable from first and irrevocable liens on the 9.0 cent per gallon county gas tax, and a 3.0 cent state gas tax. State statutes prohibit repeal or modification of the taxes that would adversely impact bondholders. The county has covenanted to maintain the 9.0 cent tax while bonds remain outstanding and has not used, nor intends to use, the state tax for these or any future debt service payments. Other legal provisions include a 1.50 times (x) additional bonds test based on historic revenues. Gas tax revenues are only available for street and highway improvements and cannot be used to fund transit systems.

Clark County continues to show strong growth and has felt few, if any, effects from competition in the gaming sector. Current population estimates are 1.1 million, a 45% increase since 1990. Fuel sales have increased about 5% annually since 1994, despite the county gas tax increase to 9.0 cents from 5.0 cents in 1995 -- part of a voter-approved funding program for transportation-related projects.

Historic debt service coverage from all pledged revenues has been strong, at least 3.57x since 1992, and 2.13x with only county taxes. Future debt service coverage is 3.15x and 2.53x, respectively. The short, 10-year maturity of the 1997 bonds reduces some concern regarding the uncertainty of future fuel sales.

Clark County, located in southern Nevada, includes the city of Las Vegas and continues to attract new residents and businesses due to the region's lower cost of living and strong job growth. Nevertheless, the economy remains heavily concentrated in gaming, with the hotel, gaming, and recreation sector providing about 26% of total county jobs in 1996. The region has been redefining itself as a destination resort for families with new hotels featuring added attractions in addition to casinos.

Currently, Las Vegas has about 101,000 hotel rooms, up from 77,000 in 1992. With the recent success of several new large resorts, a number of additional theme-oriented hotel/casino developments are planned; 20,000 rooms are now under construction and expected to be completed in 1998. Overall property values in the county are up 11.2% for fiscal 1997 to over $60 billion. Since 1990, the county's median household income level has been at national averages, due primarily to the area's affordable cost of living.
The outlook reflects the expectation that fuel purchases will continue growing at a steady pace as future growth occurs within the county, Standard & Poor's said. --U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
